papers.title: GERF: A Token-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval Framework for Schema-Guided Scientific Information Extraction
papers.abstract: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.

papers.title: MADRec: Reliable Multi-Agent Reasoning with Evidence-Grounded Debate for Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming recommender systems from conventional preference matching toward reasoning-driven and explainable decision-making. Multi-agent collaboration further advances this paradigm by distributing recommendation reasoning across specialized agents. However, existing frameworks rarely assess the reliability of intermediate reasoning during collaboration, allowing erroneous judgments to propagate across agents and ultimately degrade recommendation quality. To address this issue, we propose Multi-Agent Debate-based Recommendation (MADRec), an evidence-grounded multi-agent framework that enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning. MADRec consists of three coordinated modules. First, the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) module enables an Interaction Agent and a Semantic Agent to analyze interaction signals and content-level semantic signals from complementary perspectives, generating diverse recommendation judgments through structured debate. Second, the Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning (EG-RAR) module grounds the Semantic Agent's reasoning in item-level evidence and refines candidate scores by assessing how well the evidence supports the corresponding semantic claims. Third, the Judge-based Ranking Calibration (JRC) module leverages debate-derived reliability cues to adaptively calibrate interaction-based and semantic ranking results for the final recommendation. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MADRec consistently outperforms competitive baselines and enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning.

papers.title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.

papers.title: Structure-Exploiting Hierarchical Retrieval for Long Narrative Documents: A Precision-Oriented Alternative to Learned Abstraction Trees
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over book-length documents must locate a small, coherent set of passages inside tens of thousands of tokens. Flat dense retrieval ignores document structure; RAPTOR instead builds a hierarchy by recursively clustering and summarizing with a language model. We study a complementary design that exploits the native structure of a document: a two-level retriever that (i) selects chapters with a hybrid BM25+dense match over chapter recaps, (ii) runs a chapter-filtered dense search, and (iii) expands top passages into contiguous, section-aware spans under a token budget, plus content-hash-gated delta ingestion to keep the index cheap to update. We evaluate on five public-domain books (113 chapter-localization queries) and on QuALITY and NovelQA (200K+ token novels). In-house, we find a seed-stable precision/ranking tradeoff: with section expansion off, hierarchical retrieval returns a higher fraction of chunks from the correct chapter (+3.3pp, Wilcoxon p=0.014); with expansion on, ranking improves (MRR, p=0.040). Accuracy differences are not significant. On QuALITY, hierarchical retrieval beats flat top-k (81.0% vs 70.4%, p=0.0019) and matches the full article (p=0.74). On NovelQA, hierarchical and flat retrieval are statistically tied (55.7% vs 56.8%, p=0.24); hierarchy helps aggregation questions while flat wins on localized facts. Against a faithful RAPTOR baseline we find a complementary tradeoff, not superiority. Delta ingestion reuses 94 to 99.7% of embeddings on incremental edits. We make no claim of semantic chapter-boundary inference and scope claims to English narrative prose.

papers.title: Evaluating Memanto on DolphinBench for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost ($10.86, against $61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.

papers.title: The abc index: Exact Retrieval for Learned Sparse Representations
papers.abstract: In learned sparse retrieval (LSR), queries have tens of terms with learned weights, on which classic dynamic pruning is believed to fail, and approximate indexes such as Seismic and HNSW are considered faster than exact ones. We challenge this view with abc, an exact index built only from standard IR techniques: term-at-a-time (TAAT) evaluation, Block-Max MaxScore, binary packing and doc-id reordering. They are combined in a new design and engineered for modern CPUs. On MS MARCO encoded with four LSR models, the abc index is the fastest exact index at every k: 6.5-84x faster than the exact search of Qdrant, 13-55x faster than that of Lucene, and 2.9-18x faster than BMP with an index 5-7x smaller. Against approximate indexes, it takes 1.5-3.6x less space, and its latency grows much more slowly with k: they are up to 4.3x faster at k=10, but at k=1000 it overtakes them, by up to 7.4x. Exactness comes with an extra benefit: there are no parameters to tune.

papers.title: Who Gets Re-ranked When a Clinical Model Gains New Data?
papers.abstract: Hospitals often update a deployed risk model by adding a data source, such as laboratory results, that only some patients have. Work on safe model updates assumes fixed inputs and so ignores patients who lack the new data. The update has no new measurements for them, yet their rank can change, and a sick patient not yet tested can drop off an alert list. We split rank-based compatibility by data availability and pair it with error correction and alert-list effects. We compared each update with ordinary retraining on the old inputs, predicting ICU admission or death and hospital admission, on 78,475 emergency department visits from MC-MED and, in a pre-registered replication, 100,000 stays from MIMIC-IV-ED at a second hospital. Radiograph report text gave no detectable gain and almost no extra re-ranking. Laboratory results improved prediction but, at both hospitals and with linear or tree models, pushed patients without labs down alert lists; linear updates also reshuffled them more than retraining did, without ranking them better. A top-20% admission list caught 4.2% of admitted patients without labs after the update, against 18.8% after retraining (second hospital: 4.9% against 22.6%), while catching more patients overall. This held for list sizes from 5% to 50% and in every patient group we checked, despite better measured calibration. Separate alert thresholds for patients with and without labs restored most or all of their catch rate at both hospitals at almost no cost. Teams should check these patients before deploying such an update.
papers.comment: Accepted at the 6th International Workshop on Multi-Modal Medical Data Analysis (MMMDA), IEEE BigData 2026

papers.title: HME-PFD: Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, facilitating efficient serving of machine learning systems. In the context of ads recommendation, privileged features distillation (PFD) extends KD by allowing the teacher model to leverage privileged features, i.e., features available only during training, to enhance distillation performance. However, in real-world scenarios, privileged features often have limited coverage and exhibit heterogeneous distributions, resulting in training examples of varying importance for distillation and model learning. We propose Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation (HME-PFD), a novel approach that incorporates privileged features into the routing module of a Mixture-of-Experts-based student model. Our method introduces both hard-coded and learnable routing modules, enabling the student to dynamically determine expert assignment based on the availability and values of privileged features. This design allows the student model to better handle the heterogeneous data scenario, where privileged features are partially observed, by differentiating between high- and low-signal samples. Extensive experiments on two post-click conversion prediction tasks demonstrate that HME-PFD consistently outperforms baseline methods. Our results show that leveraging privileged features for expert routing in the student model leads to improved model performance, even when privileged features are incomplete or sparse.

papers.title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
papers.abstract: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.

papers.title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
papers.abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.

papers.title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
papers.abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

papers.title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
papers.abstract: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.

papers.title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.

papers.title: Look Before You Leap: Re-Architecting Disk-Resident Vector Search with TriVS
papers.abstract: Disk-resident approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) scales vector search beyond DRAM, yet state-of-the-art systems remain I/O-bound, even with fast SSDs and sophisticated I/O execution. To understand this bottleneck, we conduct an I/O-centric analysis that breaks each query down into an approach phase that locates a query-near region and a converge phase that resolves the final top-k. This analysis reveals complementary I/O tradeoffs: cluster-based search circumvents approach-phase I/O through in-memory routing but reads coarse-grained, full clusters during convergence, whereas graph-based search employs fine-grained, vector-level I/O throughout, enabling efficient convergence at the cost of inevitable I/O during the approach phase. To combine the complementary I/O benefits of the two granularities, we present TriVS, a new paradigm that re-architects disk-resident vector search as a trilogy: approach coarsely, distill progressively, and converge exactly. Its key innovations come in two parts. First, it decouples the approach and converge phases from a single search granularity, employing cluster-based search to avoid approach-phase I/O and leveraging vector-level I/O for efficient convergence. Second, to bridge the two granularities, it introduces a new in-memory distill phase between the original two, progressively reducing routed clusters to a vector-level shortlist using compact quantized vectors before disk access. Moreover, coarser clustering shrinks the centroid-routing index, allowing TriVS to reallocate existing memory to distillation rather than expand its memory budget. Our evaluation on five datasets spanning diverse vector types and scales shows that, at Recall@10=0.9, TriVS achieves on average 3.42X PipeANN's throughput, 51.2% lower latency, and 63.7% less disk I/O, while using less memory and storage than PipeANN.

papers.title: STUN-Bench: Truly Unseen Tools for Evaluating Shared Tool Experience
papers.abstract: A tool router retrieves a few candidate tools per request and lets a language model choose. Methods that share experience across organizations add past requests about each tool to what the router retrieves. StableToolBench calls some of its test groups tests on "unseen" tools, yet the ToolBench instruction pool, which retrievers and experience-sharing methods learn from, contains every test query and labels every gold tool of the two single-tool groups among them. We release STUN-Bench (StableToolBench, Truly UNseen), a split whose experience pool has no item that labels or names 172 held-out tools. Unseen here means absent from shared experience and retriever training data, not from pretraining. On the split we find crowding: experience pooled from five simulated clients, added to an index of tool descriptions, outranks the descriptions of tools no client has used, which then often drop out of the candidate list. Under the Jina-v2 retriever, routing accuracy on held-out tools falls from 0.534 to 0.278. Retrievers trained for tool retrieval lose much less, and keeping experience in a separate index recovers most of the loss under Jina-v2. The split also reverses a conclusion: with every test tool labeled in the pool and our default leak filter applied, shared experience beats descriptions alone; on STUN-Bench it falls below them. The split, leak filter and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/ /STUN-Bench.

papers.title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
papers.abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.

papers.title: Beyond Knowledge Transfer: How User Overlap Shapes Diversity in Cross-Domain Recommendation
papers.abstract: A common paradigm in cross-domain recommendation (CDR) transfers knowledge through users shared by source and target domains. Although this overlap bridge is effective in improving accuracy, its effect on diversity remains unclear. We identify two bottlenecks: the bridge can be too narrow when overlapping users cover limited target-domain tastes, and too loud when shared signals dominate the sparse personal evidence of non-overlapping users. To address both, we propose DivCDR, a model-agnostic Push--Pull framework. Pull constructs confidence-gated virtual positives for overlapping users and optimizes their exposure-entropy gain, broadening the preferences carried by the bridge. Push uses overlap-density-guided negative sampling to move non-overlapping users away from overlap-dense regions. Experiments on three datasets and five representative CDR backbones show that DivCDR improves recommendation diversity while preserving or improving accuracy in most settings.

papers.title: Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields with Bidirectional Diffusion Encoders for Zero-Training Cross-Ontology Medical Coding
papers.abstract: Healthcare systems continually revise clinical taxonomies, update reimbursement schedules, and harmonize cross-border registries. Existing automated coding models bind clinical text understanding to fixed vocabulary-specific heads, requiring manual relabeling and retraining whenever code sets change. We introduce Ontology-Compiled 2D Clinical State Fields (OCSF), a vocabulary-free framework that decouples clinical document reading from target ontology indexing so one trained encoder can switch across arbitrary medical vocabularies in seconds without target training. A single-pass bidirectional diffusion-pretrained encoder and vocabulary-free decoder map each clinical note into a fixed-dimension two-dimensional state matrix with zero code-specific parameters. Any target ontology is compiled offline on CPU from public text descriptions into a scale-invariant Tikhonov deconvolution operator that suppresses sibling-code interference while preserving source decision thresholds. Trained solely on English MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharge summaries and evaluated without target tuning across 58,706 held-out test notes and five unseen ontologies spanning English ICD-10, MS-DRG, Spanish, Greek, and Chinese (115-185,458 codes), OCSF reaches 63.15% Micro-F1 on in-domain ICD-9 (outperforming a matched closed-vocabulary classifier and eliminating late-epoch tail overfitting) and transfers directly to 26,085 English ICD-10 codes (29.23% recall at gold cardinality), MS-DRG groups, and multilingual terminologies, compiling up to 185,458 codes in under 10 seconds on CPU with sub-millisecond GPU readout.
papers.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 4 main tables, 5 supplementary tables. Code available at https://github.com/ZeqiangWangAI/OCSF

papers.title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
papers.abstract: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. The project is available at https://github.com/PiSchool/trallie

papers.title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
papers.abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.
papers.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at GRAIL 2026: Workshop on Generative, Retrieval-augmented, and Agentic Intelligence for Personalization, held at CIKM 2026

papers.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
papers.abstract: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

papers.title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
papers.abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

papers.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.

papers.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

papers.title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.

papers.title: RouterWeave: A Unified Observation Layer for Cross-Platform Activity Analysis via Home Routers
papers.abstract: Smart homes bring together devices from different operating systems and vendor ecosystems, but each platform reports activity only for the devices and features it supports, leaving gaps in household-wide activity monitoring. Interoperability standards such as Matter and software integrations connect and control supported devices, yet vendor restrictions and licensing barriers limit access to their data, while hardware constraints hinder integration. Our key insight is that encrypted network traffic provides complementary evidence of activity across platform boundaries. Accordingly, we present RouterWeave, a router-side observation framework that combines cross-platform traffic collection, task-adaptive processing, and unified activity records. These records preserve activity meaning, temporal extent, and source-device attribution while distinguishing discrete operations from sustained activity intervals. We evaluate RouterWeave across four datasets, native execution on a commodity home router, and two novel case studies: cross-platform Screen Time monitoring and appliance energy estimation. RouterWeave achieves 94.41% macro-F1 on application activities and 97.46% on IoT operations, outperforming baselines by up to 20.99 percentage points, while using under 7 MB of router memory per task and supporting 54 concurrent devices within a 5-second update window. In end-to-end case studies, RouterWeave reconstructs 600 Screen Time timelines across Android, iOS, and Windows with 92.15% accuracy (24.84-second mean active-time error over 19-minute averages) and recovers 49 of 55 appliance operations over four days, tracking ON/OFF states with 92.84% agreement and estimating electricity use within a 4.28% error. Together, these results establish the commodity home router as practical infrastructure for whole-home activity sensing. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/naisslab/routerweave.

papers.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
papers.abstract: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

papers.title: Modeling Attributional Style at Scale: A Dataset and Analysis for Psychological Attribution Assessment and Reframing
papers.abstract: According to the reformulated Learned Helplessness theory, repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events can foster a depressogenic attributional style, increasing susceptibility to depression yet remaining a tractable target for cognitive therapy. Computational research on attributional cognition, however, is hampered by the lack of large-scale datasets and robust evaluation protocols. In this work, we introduce the Attributional Style Transfer Dataset (ASTD) along with dedicated evaluation metrics, the first benchmark designed to model, assess, and reframe attributional explanations at scale. Constructed via a Prevent-Filter-Validate pipeline that integrates LLM-based generation with specialist validation, ASTD contains 42,000 real-world events paired with psychologically grounded attributions spanning seven styles. Using this dataset, we address two key challenges: (1) scalable assessment of attributional style via both supervised classifiers and zero/few-shot LLMs; and (2) attributional reframing and evaluation, where we propose automatic evaluation metrics to quantify psychological validity. Furthermore, we leverage our proposed metrics to construct a preference dataset, fine-tuning LLMs with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and achieving substantial gains in reframing quality. Together, our dataset, metrics, and methodology offer a new paradigm for understanding and modeling attributional style, with direct implications for scalable and adaptive mental health interventions. Code and data: https://github.com/qzhou711/ASTD

papers.title: EcomWriteBench: A Real-World Benchmark for E-commerce Writing Tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout e-commerce workflows to generate content that informs purchasing decisions and supports customer interactions. Evaluating these systems requires accounting for user needs, product evidence, structural constraints, and business requirements that are not fully captured by general-purpose writing benchmarks. We introduce EcomWriteBench, a real-world benchmark containing 3,861 queries from 69 e-commerce writing tasks across 13 categories and five languages. Through task-level extraction, cross-task consolidation, and refinement guided by human feedback, EcomWriteBench constructs a shared pool of 37 abilities and identifies the subset applicable to each task. Ability-wise scoring enables us to compare state-of-the-art LLMs on EcomWriteBench and characterize their relative strengths and weaknesses across fine-grained e-commerce writing abilities. We further propose a preference-calibrated weight-learning framework that converts human pairwise preferences into interpretable scoring rubrics through global, category-level, and task-level aggregation weights. This framework provides a reusable approach for translating human preferences into automated evaluation by combining ability discovery, ability-wise scoring, and preference-calibrated aggregation, and can potentially be applied to a broad range of benchmarks beyond EcomWriteBench. On held-out queries, our scoring framework achieves 88.96% agreement with human preferences, compared with 78.54% for conventional LLM-as-a-judge scoring.

papers.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
papers.abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

papers.title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search
papers.abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.

papers.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
papers.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

papers.title: Poisoning Attacks and Collaborative Defense Framework for LightRAG-Based Construction Regulation Knowledge
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used in construction, yet the security of building-regulation knowledge bases has received little study. This thesis reports a pre-registered experiment on one fully instrumented LightRAG system built on the UK Approved Documents. Using a 150-item benchmark labeled with safety consequences and tampering directions, it evaluates four attacks (text layer, graph layer, fabricated amendment narrative and a defense-aware adaptive attacker) together with a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design. Text-level poisoning succeeded, with success rising with the budget; graph-level poisoning was less effective, contrary to the registered hypothesis. The full defense met the registered criterion and six of the seven configurations met its threshold, but those containing the generation layer did so by refusing 69-80 percent of poisoned queries, costing up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering cost no measurable clean accuracy in the configuration used. A second experimental batch showed that excluding a legitimate unregistered amendment caused no measurable loss of accuracy either, as its wording reached the generator through the graph's entity and relationship descriptions, the route the poison took, which no layer inspects. Interactions were strong, so no layer's contribution can be isolated. A reported zero attack success rate is not evidence of detection unless the refusal rate is reported with it: zero arises either because provenance filtering removes every document outside the manifest without judging its content, or because the system refuses. Layered defenses must therefore be evaluated factorially, and regulatory RAG assistants require corpus admission control and version-aware verification before they can support safety-critical decisions.

papers.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

papers.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

papers.title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

papers.title: Same Facts, Different Decision: Fact-Invariant Manipulation and Provenance-Based Defense in Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Typed decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer only with a probability, an option, or a score, so software can act on them directly. Their inputs, however, often include text from outsiders. Prior attacks test this risk poorly. Injected instructions rarely work on these models, and added facts can make a changed decision correct. We show that outside comments can persuade these models to make a wrong decision without adding any fact. We propose LEVER, an attack that writes such comments with four levers from argumentation theory, uses a separate verifier to discard any comment that adds a fact, and searches for effective comments guided by the model's output probabilities. We further propose the Provenance Gate, a defense that accepts a changed decision only if the model reaches it again without the outside comments. On three benchmarks, LEVER flips about a third of Jev's correct decisions, 2.8 times as many as the strongest prior attack under the same limit on facts, and more on five other models. The gate blocks all of these attacks with at most one extra query and still accepts trusted updates.

papers.title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. The growing adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes another attack surface: tool descriptions supplied by third-party MCP servers. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. To address this challenge, we propose GRAFT, an LLM-based optimization method for crafting adversarial tool descriptions. Specifically, GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to identify argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection. It then iteratively refines candidate descriptions using dynamic mutation strategies proposed by an LLM, guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments. We evaluate GRAFT on three public datasets against several attack baselines. The results show that GRAFT achieves higher attack success while maintaining low detection rates across five filter-based defenses. It also bypasses several existing IPI defenses. Even under an adaptive defense trained on GRAFT-generated injections, GRAFT remains more effective than the baselines.

papers.title: Manipulation-resistant reputation for peer-to-peer scientific publishing: a combination-therapy approach
papers.abstract: In open peer-to-peer networks, where publishing is nearly free and identities are cheap, reputation systems decide what deserves attention, and their metrics become targets for manipulation. We study how to choose and combine reputation signals so that manipulation does not pay while genuine contribution does. Inspired by combination therapies in medicine, we describe each gaming action by its effects on all signals. For aggregation by the minimum of the signals, we prove that, in a global linear model, either some mix of gaming actions raises every signal by more than it costs, or the net gain of gaming is bounded by the imbalance of the attacker's honest profile; locally, gaming brings no first-order gain exactly when an admissible weighting is supported on the attacker's weakest signals. We then specify, without implementing it, MagMell, a two-tier system for peer-to-peer scientific publication: a protocol that orders signed events by Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus, enforces budgets and settles staked assessments, and open reputation algorithms that any node can run. Simulations on synthetic data show that minimum aggregation makes networks of fake identities, collusion rings and floods of generated papers lose rank beyond small intensities, at the price of a lower correlation between rank and quality for honest accounts. They also show that criticism is rarely settled, because the evidence needed is seldom available. The replicated log should grow by about 26 kilobytes per identity and year (analytic estimate), and a full recomputation of reputations takes 1.0 to 1.6 seconds for 100,000 identities (measured).

papers.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

papers.title: Pre-Crawl Prioritization and Seed Classification for Large-Scale Web Archiving
papers.abstract: Pre-crawl prioritization systems decide which pages to fetch first before indexing, aiming to improve crawl efficiency and coverage. Existing approaches based on page popularity and relevance are unsuited to web-archival crawlers that prioritize comprehensive coverage over selective retrieval. We explore prioritization techniques tailored to web archival operations using URL lexical analysis, dynamic domain reputation systems, and HTTP response analysis to inform crawl scheduling decisions. By incorporating predictive models that estimate content change and disappearance probabilities, we improve crawl completeness while reducing redundant visits to stable resources. Through large-scale experiments, we demonstrate that our methods improve archival effectiveness and resource utilization compared to undirected crawling.

papers.title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
papers.abstract: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.
